primary_topics: Chapter 11 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's survey of the labor (NLRC) ponencias he wrote in his first three years on the Supreme Court (October 10, 1995 to October 10, 1998), all unanimously supported, offered as his working answer to how a judge finds 'the right balance between labor and management' under a Constitution that guarantees full protection to labor and a rule that in case of doubt the law favors labor.

The employer's burden of proof: San Pedro Hospital and Somerville Stainless Steel both turn on documentary evidence -- an employer who claims a precarious financial condition, a bona fide suspension of operations or a need to retrench must prove it convincingly, not merely allege it.

The limits of pro-labor doctrine: North Davao Mining (no separation pay from a company killed by over P20 billion in losses) and Philippines Today (an abrasive memorandum to the CEO, read with confirmatory acts, as voluntary resignation) show CJP ruling for management where the facts compel it, on the principle that 'General principles do not decide specific cases.'

Who is an employer and who is an employee: Naguiat holds the owner who actively manages a close corporation solidarily liable for separation pay as a corporate tort, and Caurdanetaan applies the 'four fold' test -- hire, wages, dismissal and, most important, control -- to declare cargadores regular employees.

Procedural and remedial convictions running through the set: the Court should resolve the whole controversy rather than remand, the employer always carries the burden of proof in illegal dismissal, and dismissal in bad faith and without the two required notices justifies moral damages and attorney's fees.
sub_topics: CJP frames the chapter: before St. Martin Funeral Home v. NLRC the Supreme Court entertained certiorari petitions against NLRC decisions directly, and finding the right balance in those reviews 'can sometimes become really contentious,' though the Constitution guarantees full protection to labor and in case of doubt the law favors labor.

A. San Pedro Hospital v. Secretary of Labor: after a deadlock over a P60 versus P2 increase and a union security clause, the union struck, the labor secretary assumed jurisdiction and ordered a return to work, and the hospital instead declared a six-month suspension of operations.

The Court held the suspension invalid: temporary suspension is a valid management prerogative only if not used to circumvent the Labor Code or defeat employees' rights, the burden of proving good faith is the employer's, and the hospital's 'unexplained and continued failure to submit its financial statements' raised grave doubts about the claimed crisis.

It also held the secretary could order a new CBA and grant back wages without first ruling on the legality of the strike -- the employment relationship is only suspended, and Article 263(g) and (i) let him penalize an employer who refused to accept returning workers.

B. North Davao Mining v. APT: a company forced to close by accumulated losses of over P20 billion owes no separation benefits, not even to match its own longstanding 30-day-per-year practice, because Article 283 imposes the obligation only where closure is not due to serious business losses.

CJP distinguishes BISSI, where the closing employer could still afford (and paid) more generous separation pay to the last batch, from North Davao, where 'upon its death as a going business concern, its vital lifeblood -- its cashflow -- literally dries up.'

C. Philippines Today v. NLRC: Felix R. Alegre Jr.'s memorandum to chairman Betty Go-Belmonte, airing his frustrations and differences with publisher Maximo V. Soliven, was held to constitute voluntary resignation -- an exception to the general rule -- given its offensive wording, its circulation to the whole board and his status as a confidential employee.

The confirmatory acts mattered most: an unproven medical reason for his leave, his clearing his desk of personal belongings, his failure to return after the leave expired, and his taking a higher-paying job as chief of staff to Senator Sotero H. Laurel before the resignation was accepted.

CJP reproduces the Epilogue to stress that the Court 'does not matter-of-factly apply and interpret laws in a vacuum' -- each case 'has its own flesh and blood and cannot be decided simply on the basis of isolated clinical classroom principles.'

D. Naguiat v. NLRC: taxi drivers of Clark Field Taxi, Inc., displaced by the phase-out of the US bases and not by losses, were entitled to regular Article 283 separation pay, their boundary earnings being inferable at not less than $240 a month absent contrary proof.

On solidary liability, only the owner actively engaged in management -- Naguiat, the president who actively ran CFTI -- was held personally liable, under Article 212(c) of the Labor Code and Section 100(5) of the Corporation Code on close corporations, the failure to pay separation pay being a breach of a legal duty, that is, a tort.

E. Caurdanetaan Piece Workers Union v. Laguesma: applying the 'four fold' test -- power to hire, payment of wages, power to dismiss and, most important, power to control -- the cargadores who loaded and piled sacks of palay for Corfarm were regular employees under Article 280, not independent contractors.

CJP refused to follow the NLRC's remand to the labor arbiter, invoking the duty to settle the entire controversy in a single proceeding 'leaving no root or branch to bear the seeds of future litigation,' and noting that in illegal dismissal cases 'the employer always has the burden of proof.'

F. Somerville Stainless Steel v. NLRC: a single 1992 financial statement showing a P392,996.38 total loss fell 'far short of the stringent requirement of the law,' since it did not show whether losses were rising or falling -- contrasted with AG&P's multi-year decline and North Davao's P3-billion-a-year average losses.

G. Pascua v. NLRC: resignation must be voluntary and accompanied by an intention and an act of relinquishment; allowing dismissal on mere allegations and generalizations would place employees 'at the mercy' of employers and emasculate security of tenure.

Pascua also awarded moral damages and attorney's fees because Henry Lao's dismissals were 'marked by precipitate dispatch and utter disregard of due process,' the Court restating the two-notice rule -- notice of intention to dismiss, opportunity to answer, then notice of the decision.

stances.claim: An employer who invokes losses -- to justify a suspension of operations, a closure or a retrenchment -- must prove them convincingly with financial evidence, and the burden never shifts to the workers.
stances.rhetorical_move: evidentiary-burden test applied comparatively across San Pedro Hospital, Somerville and AG&P

stances.claim: Where a business has truly died of its losses -- over P20 billion in North Davao's case -- the law imposes no separation pay, because 'one cannot squeeze blood out of a dry stone.'
stances.rhetorical_move: proverbial image distinguishing a going concern from a dead one, used to limit the BISSI precedent

stances.claim: Although the Constitution and the Labor Code mandate a bias in favor of labor, a case is decided on its own peculiar facts -- 'General principles do not decide specific cases.'
stances.rhetorical_move: epilogue restatement of judicial method, conceding the pro-labor tilt before carving the exception

stances.claim: Courts should resolve the entire controversy in a single proceeding rather than remand, so that justice is not needlessly delayed.
stances.rhetorical_move: speedy-justice principle invoked to refuse the NLRC's remand in Caurdanetaan

notable_anecdotes: CJP marks the period he is accounting for -- his 'first three years in office (October 10, 1995 to October 10, 1998)' -- and notes that the labor decisions he discusses were unanimously supported by the other members of the Court.

He recounts the San Pedro Hospital standoff in which the union's picket halted operations, forcing doctors and patients to leave the site, and the hospital then refused to readmit workers who were willing to return.

He retells the Philippine Star episode: Alegre's memorandum to Betty Go-Belmonte, copied to every officer and board member, and the acts that betrayed his intent -- clearing his desk of personal belongings and taking a better-paid job in a senator's office before his resignation was even accepted.
He reproduces the Epilogue of Philippines Today in full to explain why he departed from the general rule, insisting that the Court 'does not matter-of-factly apply and interpret laws in a vacuum.'
He records the Caurdanetaan aside -- 'Why Respondent NLRC refused to rule directly on the appeal escapes us' -- as his objection to a remand in a case already pending since 1992.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' gathered the labor rulings Artemio V. Panganiban wrote in his first three years on the Supreme Court (October 10, 1995 to October 10, 1998), all unanimously supported, as his answer to how a judge finds the right balance between labor and management -- a search he called contentious even though the Constitution guarantees full protection to labor and, in case of doubt, the law favors labor. In San Pedro Hospital v. Secretary of Labor he held a six-month suspension of operations invalid because the hospital's unexplained failure to submit financial statements left its claimed crisis unproven, and upheld the labor secretary's power to order a new CBA with a union security clause and to grant back wages without first ruling on the strike's legality. In North Davao Mining v. APT he denied separation benefits to workers of a company killed by over P20 billion in losses, distinguishing BISSI on the ground that when a business dies its cashflow 'literally dries up' and 'one cannot squeeze blood out of a dry stone.' Philippines Today treated Felix Alegre's abrasive memorandum to the Star's chairman, read with his clearing of his desk and his acceptance of a senator's job, as voluntary resignation, its Epilogue insisting that 'General principles do not decide specific cases' and that each case 'has its own flesh and blood.' Naguiat awarded regular separation pay to Clark taxi drivers displaced by the bases phase-out and held the actively managing owner solidarily liable for the corporate tort; Caurdanetaan applied the 'four fold' test to declare cargadores regular employees and refused the NLRC's remand, invoking the duty to leave 'no root or branch to bear the seeds of future litigation'; Somerville rejected a lone year's financial statement as proof of retrenchment-justifying losses; and Pascua awarded moral damages and attorney's fees for dismissals marked by precipitate dispatch and utter disregard of due process.
